content: Midwives play a critical role in supervising community health workers (CHWs) who provide palliative care. They are instrumental in delivering palliative care that does not involve prescribing medications and in triaging patients who may require a physician's attention. Midwives are also essential in providing palliative care for critically ill neonates and offering emotional support to their parents. Their ability to prescribe medications depends on their level of training and local licensing laws. However, they can be trained to recognize moderate or severe distress in neonates and to transport patients in need of palliative care to the nearest health center or facility capable of providing such care. Clinicians trained in basic pediatric palliative care (PPC) may occasionally encounter physical or psychological suffering that they feel unable to adequately address. In some settings, referral to specialized PPC may not be feasible. Examples of such challenges include pain that is unresponsive to high-dose morphine, depression resistant to maximum-dose SSRIs, or psychotic disorders. In cases where referral is not possible, clinicians with palliative care training should utilize available resources, such as a palliative care hotline or telemedicine services, to provide the best possible care under the circumstances rather than refusing to treat the patient. CHWs can play a vital role in palliative care and symptom management by frequently visiting patients and families at home and assisting them in navigating the local healthcare system. With as little as three to six hours of palliative care training, CHWs can provide emotional support, recognize uncontrolled symptoms, identify unmet basic needs such as food, shelter, or clothing, and detect improper use of medications. They can report their findings to a nurse supervisor at a health center, enabling appropriate responses such as changes in prescriptions or home visits by a nurse, which may eliminate the need for the patient to return to a hospital or health center. These visits also help reduce the emotional, physical, and financial burdens often experienced by family caregivers. Family caregivers, who are often women with additional work and childcare responsibilities, should be trained, equipped, and encouraged by clinicians to provide basic nursing care, such as wound and oral care and medication administration. However, clinicians should assess and address the unmet social needs of these caregivers, who frequently live in poverty. Clinicians should also routinely ask patients with serious or life-limiting health conditions, or their families, if they desire spiritual counseling. Efforts should be made to facilitate access to culturally appropriate spiritual counseling provided by local volunteers, tailored to the beliefs and needs of the patient and family. Social support for patients and family caregivers living in extreme poverty is essential to ensure their basic needs, such as food, housing, and transportation to medical care, are met and to promote dignity. This support may include basic food packages, cash payments for housing or school fees, transportation vouchers for clinic or hospital visits, and in-kind support such as blankets, sleeping mats, shoes, soap, toothbrushes, and toothpaste. Additionally, locally appropriate funeral costs should be accessible to families living in extreme poverty, as the inability to provide a culturally appropriate burial can become a chronic emotional burden. Efforts to rescue severely malnourished children should be combined with palliative care to maximize their comfort and provide psychosocial support for their families. Treating adverse effects of refeeding, such as vomiting and diarrhea, not only provides comfort but may also improve survival. The pain or dyspnea of dying children should be relieved, and their parents should receive emotional support. Neonates and preverbal children are particularly vulnerable due to their inability to communicate their suffering. Critically ill neonates are especially at risk because many neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) focus solely on life-sustaining treatments without integrating palliative care. However, critical care and palliative care are not mutually exclusive and should be integrated to maximize the comfort of both the patient and their parents. In settings where state-of-the-art NICUs are unavailable, neonates born after longer gestation or at higher birth weights who may not survive should receive palliative care. Palliative care should also be provided for children born with life-limiting abnormalities or malformations and should begin immediately for family support when such conditions are discovered during pregnancy or at birth, including in cases of stillbirth. Midwives or traditional birth attendants can play an important role in providing palliative care when a life-limiting fetal anomaly is diagnosed during pregnancy or when a stillbirth occurs. They can offer emotional support and advise parents on spending time with their dying baby or holding a stillborn baby, creating cherished memories such as photographs or handprints, and organizing culturally appropriate rituals such as baptisms or wakes. Policies and procedures for obstetrical, neonatal, and palliative care should guide the roles of midwives and traditional birth attendants, who should receive basic training in PPC and be welcomed as members of palliative care teams. Clinicians should ensure that dying children are placed in quiet and private locations, with provisions made for family presence. The understanding of the prognosis by the patient or family should be gently explored and corrected as needed, in a culturally appropriate manner. Bad news should be conveyed in a way that is suitable for the patient’s developmental stage and the family’s culture and history. It should be emphasized that there is no intention to hasten death, but every effort will be made to ensure comfort at all times. Intensive efforts must be made to relieve pain and other symptoms, as comfort-oriented care often requires ingenuity and dedication comparable to critical care. Bereavement support should be accessible as needed after a stillbirth or the death of any neonate or child. Bereaved adults and children without mental disorders should receive general care principles, including communication, mobilizing social support, and attention to overall well-being. Psychological first aid, as defined by the WHO, should be offered, and participation in culturally appropriate mourning practices should be encouraged and facilitated. Bereavement support groups led by adequately trained personnel may also be helpful. Efforts to integrate PPC into healthcare systems should follow a public health strategy to ensure cost-effective access for all in need. National healthcare policies must mandate palliative care services, including access to pain control with opioid medications, to make PPC widely accessible and sustainable. Training programs for PPC should be developed and implemented, starting with basic training for primary care physicians and those frequently caring for children with serious or life-threatening conditions. Physicians completing basic PPC training should be empowered to prescribe oral and injectable morphine for both inpatients and outpatients. Training should also extend to practicing nurses and be integrated into undergraduate medical, nursing, and pharmacy curricula. PPC services should be integrated into existing healthcare delivery systems, starting at any level where the need is most apparent, such as cancer centers. Initial services may include inpatient wards, consultation services, or outpatient clinics. National policies should require PPC services at all cancer centers and, over time, at all levels of the healthcare system, including secondary and tertiary hospitals, district hospitals, community health centers, and home care settings.
